issues.legal_issue: An appeal under the ordinary civil appeal procedure is not maintainable against a consent decree.
material_facts: A civil court disposed of the landlords’ possession suit as settled and passed a decree on the parties’ recorded statements.
A defendant challenged the consent decree by filing an appeal rather than pursuing her application before the court that recorded the compromise.
issues.conclusion: The appeal against the consent decree was not maintainable; a party seeking to avoid such a decree must approach the court that recorded the compromise and establish that there was no valid compromise.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 96(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, no appeal lies from a decree passed with the parties’ consent. Order 43 Rule 1(m) was deleted, and Order 23 Rule 3A bars an independent suit to set aside a compromise decree on the ground that the compromise was unlawful. The court that recorded the compromise may decide, under the proviso to Order 23 Rule 3, whether a valid compromise existed. The Court allowed the jurisdictional objection to be raised for the first time on appeal, relying on Shanti Devi v. Bimla Devi, Zahoor v. State of U.P., and Hiralal v. Kasturi Devi.

predicates.appeal_against_consent_decree: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decree that was passed with the parties’ consent.
predicates.challenge_brought_by_appeal: The party seeks to set aside the consent decree by appeal rather than by applying to the court that recorded the compromise.

issues.definition: When a party appeals a decree passed with consent instead of applying to the court that recorded the compromise, the appeal is not maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: A settlement requiring a tenant to perform an obligation in the future is an enforceable compromise, not a completed satisfaction of the plaintiff’s claim.
material_facts: The suit sought possession of premises from a tenant.
Under the settlement, the tenant undertook to vacate the premises on a future date and to pay rent or damages until then.
The resulting decree could be enforced if the tenant failed to vacate as promised.
issues.conclusion: The settlement fell within the part of Order 23 Rule 3 that applies to a written compromise signed by the parties, not the part concerning an already completed satisfaction of the claim.
issues.legal_principle: Order 23 Rule 3 distinguishes a written agreement or compromise containing promises that can be enforced by execution from a completed satisfaction or settlement that leaves nothing to be performed. A future undertaking to vacate premises is enforceable by execution and therefore belongs to the former category; a report that the tenant has already vacated, or that the plaintiff will not press the possession claim, is a completed satisfaction. No earlier case was necessary to this distinction.

predicates.possession_suit_against_tenant: The proceeding is a suit by a landlord seeking possession from a tenant.
predicates.settlement_requires_future_performance: The settlement requires the tenant to perform an obligation in the future, rather than recording that the claim has already been satisfied.

issues.definition: In a landlord’s possession suit, a settlement requiring future performance is an enforceable promise rather than a completed satisfaction.

issues.legal_issue: Statements of duly authorized counsel, recorded in writing and signed by counsel, can satisfy the written-and-signed requirements for a lawful compromise.
material_facts: The defendant had authorized her counsel to act in the suit and enter into a compromise.
The counsel for both sides made statements on oath specifying the settlement terms; the court recorded the statements in writing, and the counsel read, accepted, and signed them.
The settlement terms were lawful and required the tenant to vacate the premises in the future.
The defendant’s evidence had been closed after repeated opportunities, and the settlement was made when no further evidence was tendered.
issues.conclusion: The recorded and signed statements of the authorized counsel satisfied the requirements for a written compromise, and the consent decree was valid. The Court also noted that the circumstances supported treating the decree as based on the defendants’ admissions.
issues.legal_principle: Order 23 Rule 3 requires a lawful compromise to be in writing and signed by the parties. Read with Order 3 Rules 1 and 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, “parties” includes duly authorized pleaders acting for them; the parties need not sign personally. Statements recorded in writing by the court and signed by the persons making them are a writing for this purpose, consistent with the definition of “document” in Section 3 of the Evidence Act. The Court applied Byram Pestonji Gariwala v. Union Bank of India and Jineshwardas v. Jagrani, distinguished Gurpreet Singh v. Chatur Bhuj Goel, and referred to Smt. Jamilabai Abdul Kadar v. Shankarlal Gulabchand concerning counsel acting for a client in the circumstances. Jineshwardas also recognizes that a decree following consensus may be a judgment on admission.

rule.if: suit_resolved_by_compromise and counsel_authorized_to_compromise and terms_recorded_in_writing and recorded_terms_signed_by_counsel and terms_lawful

predicates.suit_resolved_by_compromise: The parties resolve a civil suit through a compromise presented to the court.
predicates.counsel_authorized_to_compromise: A party has authorized counsel to act for the party and enter into a compromise in the proceeding.
predicates.terms_recorded_in_writing: The court records the specific compromise terms in writing after they are stated before it.
predicates.recorded_terms_signed_by_counsel: The counsel making the recorded statements accepts them as correct and signs them.

issues.definition: A compromise is valid as a written compromise when it resolves a suit, is made by authorized counsel, is recorded in writing and signed by counsel, and has lawful terms.
